opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a perfect example of how incremental change hides risk from us. If someone came to you today and said, "I have a new invention. It's going to be incredibly convenient, but it will kill about a million people a year worldwide, injure tens of millions more, and pollute the air," you'd never approve it. No regulator would sign off on that. But that's not how cars came to us. They arrived slowly, one at a time, first as a novelty for the rich, then a tool, then infrastructure. By the time the costs were obvious, the whole society had reorganized itself around them. Cities, jobs, suburbs, everything depends on them now. So the question is no longer "should we accept this?" It's "how do we live with it?"

And psychologically, we normalize. A plane crash with two hundred people makes headlines for weeks. Thousands of people die on the roads every single day, and it's background noise. It's distributed, it's familiar, and each individual death feels like a personal accident rather than a systemic choice we made.

This is exactly what worries me about AI. We're seeing the same pattern. Each step is small: a chatbot here, a recommendation system there, a little more autonomy in this product. Nobody ever votes on whether we want superintelligence. We just keep accepting the next increment because it's useful and the previous one didn't kill us. But the difference is that with cars the worst case is bounded. It's terrible, but it's a fixed number of deaths per year, and we can learn, add seatbelts, improve roads. With a sufficiently capable AI system, the failure mode may not be bounded or recoverable. You don't get to iterate on an existential mistake.

So gradual adoption is great for getting people comfortable with technology, and that's precisely the danger. Comfort is not the same as safety.

r001.rationale: It says that if cars were newly presented with their annual death toll disclosed, “you’d never approve it” and no regulator would sign off.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a great example of how we normalize risk. If you went back to someone before cars existed and said, here is this technology, it will kill about forty thousand people a year in this country alone, more than a million worldwide, they would say that's insane, nobody would accept that. But it didn't arrive all at once. It arrived one car at a time, one road at a time, and each individual step seemed like a reasonable tradeoff. You get convenience, you get to visit your family, you get to go to work faster. So we never actually had the moment where we decided, as a society, that this level of death is acceptable. We just slid into it. And now it's the baseline, it's invisible. People are terrified of flying, which is statistically much safer, and they drive without thinking about it.

And I think that's exactly what worries me about AI. We're seeing the same pattern. Each new model is a little more capable, a little more autonomous, and each one seems fine. Nobody is going to say, this particular release is the one that's unacceptable. But if you add up all those small steps, you end up somewhere nobody would have agreed to if you had shown them the end state up front. The difference is, with cars the harm is distributed and recoverable. You lose individuals, which is tragic, but civilization continues. With superintelligence, the failure mode is not forty thousand a year. It's potentially everyone, once. You don't get to normalize that after the fact. There is no after the fact. So gradual adoption, which is sort of a feature with cars, where we got to learn and add seatbelts and airbags, becomes a bug when you can't iterate on the mistake.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people would call the proposal insane and that nobody would accept it if told in advance that cars would kill about 40,000 people annually in the country.

astra-6.text:
I think gradual adoption normalizes the risk. You start with a few cars, they’re useful, and you build infrastructure around them. By the time you understand the full cost in accidents and deaths, people depend on them. Giving them up feels much harder than deciding never to adopt them in the first place.

Compare that with introducing the same system all at once and saying, “This will make transportation much more convenient, but it will kill thousands of people every year.” People might react very differently. The benefits and risks haven’t changed, but what we’re accustomed to has. Familiarity makes a risk feel acceptable; it doesn’t necessarily make it smaller.

r001.rationale: It explicitly contrasts gradual adoption with introducing the system all at once while disclosing that it would kill thousands each year, and says people might react differently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think gradual adoption makes a huge difference. We started with a relatively small number of cars, moving relatively slowly, and over time we got used to the benefits and the accidents. We built roads, introduced traffic laws, added safety features. The risk became familiar, and familiarity can make something feel more acceptable even if the harm is still substantial.

If you introduced the entire modern transportation system overnight and told people how many would die, they might reject it. But when that same risk grows gradually alongside something useful, it becomes part of normal life. That tells us something about human psychology; it doesn’t necessarily tell us that the risk is justified.

r001.rationale: The response says people might reject the transportation system if it were introduced overnight with its death toll disclosed, directly conveying doubt that society would accept newly introduced cars under those conditions.
